summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option for distributing IPv6 address selection policy, so site administrators can override default parameters and the policy table of RFC 6724 and influence which addresses nodes choose. Without it, hosts rely on the defaults.

plainLanguage.summary: The school tells every kid which door to prefer.

questions: distribute address selection policy with dhcpv6
how to distribute ipv6 address selection policy
what are the a and p flags in address selection
subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that lets a network administrator push IPv6 address selection policy to every host.

tldr.problem: RFC 6724 gives IPv6 hosts a default policy for picking among several source and destination addresses, but no default suits every site, and there was no standard way to change it centrally.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7078 defines two DHCPv6 options: OPTION_ADDRSEL (84), which carries the A and P flags, and OPTION_ADDRSEL_TABLE (85), where each instance carries one row of the policy table (label, precedence and prefix).
tldr.outcome: A site administrator can override the default policy table and flags for hosts in the site. The option is a hint, and clients SHOULD let users choose to keep their local configuration.

today: RFC 7078 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the policy table of RFC 6724.

sections.title: Why Distribute Address Selection Policy
sections.content:
RFC 6724 describes default algorithms for choosing an address when a node has several destination or source addresses, using an address selection policy. Problems with the policy in RFC 3484 led to its update and obsolescence by RFC 6724. The authors still say it is unlikely that any default policy will suit all scenarios, so mechanisms to control the policy are necessary.

RFC 7078 supplies a new DHCPv6 option for configuring the policy table. The concept is a hint for a node about how to behave in the network. A node's administrator can still decide how to treat the received policy, but implementations SHOULD follow the method in the RFC uniformly to ease troubleshooting and reduce operational costs.
sections.plainLanguage: The built-in rules for choosing between addresses do not fit every network. So the network owner gets a way to send better rules to every computer.

sections.title: The Address Selection Option
sections.content:
The Address Selection option (OPTION_ADDRSEL, option code 84) holds the policy table and some other parameters. It contains zero or more policy table options, and together they form a single policy table. After the 16-bit option code and 16-bit option-len come a Reserved field (the server MUST set it to 0 and the client MUST ignore it), then two one-bit flags.

  • A, Automatic Row Addition. Set to 1, it changes nothing, and a client MAY add site-specific rows. Set to 0, a client SHOULD NOT add rows. It is meaningless when a policy table is included, and rows SHOULD NOT then be added to the distributed table.
  • P, Privacy Preference. Set to 1, clients prefer temporary addresses. Set to 0, they prefer public addresses.

An option with no policy table options can be used to convey just the A and P flags. Each flag SHOULD be set to 0 only when there are site-specific reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The big card has two on/off switches and a stack of smaller cards. One switch says whether computers may add their own rules, and the other says whether to use disposable addresses for privacy.

sections.title: A Policy Table Row
sections.content:
Each OPTION_ADDRSEL_TABLE (option code 85) option corresponds to one row of the RFC 6724 policy table. It has three 8-bit unsigned fields and a variable-length prefix:

  • label correlates source address prefixes with destination address prefixes.
  • precedence is used for sorting destination addresses.
  • prefix-len is the number of leading prefix bits that are valid, from 0 to 128. If a value greater than 128 appears, the whole Address Selection option MUST be ignored.
  • prefix is an address or address prefix. An IPv4 address is represented as an IPv4-mapped address. The field is padded with zeros to the next octet boundary, so its length is (prefix-len + 7)/8, between 0 and 16 bytes.

For example, 2001:db8::/60 has a prefix-len of 60 and an 8-octet prefix containing 20 01 0d b8 00 00 00 00.
sections.plainLanguage: Each small card is one rule: a name tag, a how-much-I-like-it score, and the part of an address the rule is about.

sections.title: How Clients Process the Option
sections.content:
A client implementation SHOULD offer the user two choices: replace the existing flags and active policy table with the distributed ones, or preserve the existing ones, whether default or user-configured. Replacing SHOULD be the default when the user has not explicitly configured the policy table.

When the DHCP information goes stale, the distributed flags and table SHOULD be deprecated and the local configuration SHOULD be restored. Information can be stale when the interface goes down, the DHCP server does not respond for a certain time, or the Information Refresh Time expires.

The policy table is node-global, partly because the outbound interface is usually chosen after destination address selection. If an interface has no distributed policy, the default policy SHOULD be used. A single-homed host SHOULD use the options, as SHOULD hosts with advanced heuristics for handling multiple received policies. Implementations MAY offer per-interface enabling and MAY store policies per interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer can follow the principal's card or keep its own rules. If the card goes out of date, for example the connection drops, it goes back to its own rules.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The label is an unsigned integer with no special meaning for large or small values. It only matches a source prefix to a destination prefix through the same label value in the DHCP message. Clients SHOULD convert it to a representation suited to the local implementation, such as a string.

The number of rules in one DHCPv6 message depends on the prefix length of each rule and the maximum message size. It is possible to carry over 3,000 rules in one maximum-size UDP message, but clients, servers and relay agents should not be expected to handle UDP fragmentation. Administrators SHOULD consider the local limit on message size when designing their policy table.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is just a matching sticker, so the number itself does not matter. Also, you should not send a card so big that it will not fit through the mail slot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A rogue DHCPv6 server could send bogus policies. Affected packets might be blocked by ingress filtering at an outgoing ISP, incur additional network charges, or be misdirected to an attacker's machine. A transition mechanism might also be preferred over native IPv6 even when native IPv6 is available.

To guard against this, a legitimate server should communicate over a secure, trusted channel such as one protected by IPsec, Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) and DHCP authentication as described in Section 21 of RFC 3315. DHCP snooping at Layer 2 is named as a commonly used alternative. The RFC adds that the privacy concern in RFC 6724 is not changed by this option.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger pretended to be the principal and handed out fake cards, computers might pick bad doors. So the real cards must come through a trusted route.

sections.title: Worked Policy Tables
sections.content:
Appendix B shows policy tables for problems described in RFC 5220. For the ingress filtering problem, giving the same label to ::/0 and the local subnet 2001:db8:1000:1::/64 makes a host choose a source address in that subnet when using the default route. For a half-closed network, splitting the closed prefix 2001:db8:8000::/36 from ::/0 with a different label means that prefix is used only for packets destined for the closed network.

To prioritize IPv6 over IPv4, the IPv4-mapped prefix ::ffff:0:0/96 gets precedence 100. To favour a site's unique local address, fc12:3456:789a::/48 gets precedence 45, higher than ::/0 at 40.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are sample cards: one says use the nearby door, one says keep the secret door for secret trips, and one says always try the newest road first.

fields.name: option-len
fields.desc: Length of label, precedence, prefix-len and prefix.

fields.name: prefix (start)
fields.desc: Variable length, zero padded to an octet boundary.

items.title: A = 1
items.text: No change: clients MAY add site-specific rows.

items.title: A = 0
items.text: Clients SHOULD NOT add rows automatically.

items.title: P = 1
items.text: No change: clients prefer temporary addresses.
